m4.reason: userspace data path refuted by direct measurement: a userspace read lands block-device bytes in host pages before any userspace code can move them, so it is the host bounce the project exists to remove. The card's core (real NVMe bytes in VRAM with nothing else in the loop) requires a kernel-side DMA path.
m4.kernel_dma_path: BUILT and MEASURED on Intel Arc (Arc Pro B60): NVMe controller DMA lands disk bytes in a GPU-owned VRAM BO, consumed by an OpenCL kernel, via_host_bounce=0. Raw output in results/. Superseded the earlier 'UNBUILT and UNMEASURED' entry at 0.0.1.
m4.gain_scope: Deliberately still false at 0.0.1, and not a contradiction of the numbers in kernel_dma_engine. What is measured is a TRANSFER gain on a microbenchmark: 2.91 GB/s cold vs a host-fed 1.58 GB/s, at 16.3x less CPU per GiB. What is NOT demonstrated is an INFERENCE gain -- no engine consumes arcwell yet, and per-expert latency (1.125 ms) exceeds the CPU compute it would hide behind (198 us), so a naive synchronous integration would be SLOWER. The async surface exists for prefetch; that it hides the latency is unproven. gain_demonstrated flips only when an inference engine is measured end to end.
m4.next: Integration. The engine is built and measured; the open question is whether prefetch through AW_IOC_SUBMIT_BATCH / AW_IOC_BATCH_WAIT hides the per-expert latency inside a real decode loop. See docs/USING_ARCWELL.md. (The A770 leg named by the earlier value of this field was backlogged by operator decision; work proceeds on the B60.)
m4.api_decision: v2: PRIMARY = expert streaming to VRAM for inference. One AW_IOC_MAP_BUFFER per VRAM buffer registered once at load, then one AW_IOC_READ_BLOCKS per expert weight buffer (MoE hot path). aw_write demoted to SECONDARY, off the inference path. Contract is the ioctl uAPI, not a client library.
m4.kernel_dma_engine: BUILT -- stub/src/arcwell.c implements the Intel xe + NVMe p2pdma path (dma-buf dynamic attach with peer2peer, iommu_iova_to_phys, pci_p2pdma_add_resource, bio submission). The ioctl contract is not the engine; the engine now exists. Measured 2.91 GB/s cold against a host-fed 1.58 GB/s, at 16.3x less CPU per GiB.
m4.fiemap_resolution: direct path is RAW NVMe BLOCK -> VRAM; FIEMAP (filesystem ioctl) ABSENT from the data path; at most ONE open-time translation (file -> block ranges) if experts are addressed as files; NEVER per-read. Neither filesystem in the fleet provides extents (ZFS: none; btrfs: EOPNOTSUPP).
m4.ioctl_surface: NO custom aw_set_fiemap ioctl -- FIEMAP is the standard FS_IOC_FIEMAP ioctl where used at all. The module's custom surface is the DMA-mapping/registration path: AW_IOC_MAP_BUFFER (register a VRAM buffer as an NVMe DMA target) + AW_IOC_READ_BLOCKS (issue storage->VRAM DMA). Raw-block model: ioctls take raw block ranges.
m4.layout_decision: BOTH layouts work. (A) experts as parts of one file: FIEMAP once for the whole file, per-expert offset -> translate into the file's block extents; but an expert can SPAN a file-extent boundary -> module must split the DMA into multi-segment reads. (B) one file per expert, continuous blocks: each expert is usually ONE contiguous block range -> one contiguous DMA per expert, no extent-splitting; cost = register + FIEMAP per expert at load. RECOMMENDATION: one-file-per-expert is the cleaner layout for direct block->VRAM. Honest caveat: 'continuous blocks' is best-effort — contiguity is what FIEMAP reports (ZFS may not guarantee it); the module handles actual extents.
